questions.question: What is the exception class hierarchy in Java?
questions.title: Java Exception Class Hierarchy Explained
questions.direct_answer: **`Throwable`** is the root of everything you can throw in Java. It has two direct children: **`Error`** (serious JVM problems like `OutOfMemoryError` you shouldn't catch) and **`Exception`** (recoverable conditions). **`RuntimeException`** sits under `Exception` and is the parent of all **unchecked** exceptions, while every other `Exception` subclass is **checked** — the compiler forces you to handle or declare it.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know Throwable — not Exception — is the root, and can place Error, Exception, and RuntimeException correctly while explaining checked vs unchecked
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying Exception is the root of the hierarchy, or thinking 'RuntimeException' means it happens at runtime rather than meaning 'unchecked'
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Draw the tree from Throwable down, then explain that the checked/unchecked split is a compiler rule layered on top of it — Error and RuntimeException are both unchecked but for opposite reasons

sections.title: The Exception Hierarchy, Rooted at Throwable
sections.content:
Java's exception system is a normal class hierarchy, and the class at the very top is **`Throwable`** — not `Exception`, which is the single most common fresher mistake. Only a `Throwable` (or a subclass) can appear in a `throw` statement or a `catch` clause.

`Throwable` has exactly two direct subclasses:

- **`Error`** — serious problems raised by the JVM itself, like `OutOfMemoryError` or `StackOverflowError`. Your code normally can't recover from these, so you don't catch them.
- **`Exception`** — conditions a program can reasonably anticipate and handle, like a missing file (`IOException`) or a failed query (`SQLException`).

Under `Exception` lives a special subclass, **`RuntimeException`**, the parent of every **unchecked** exception (`NullPointerException`, `IllegalArgumentException`). Everything else under `Exception` is **checked** — the compiler refuses to build until you either `catch` it or declare it with `throws`. So the hierarchy and the checked/unchecked rule are two different things layered together.

sections.title: The Throwable Family Tree
sections.content:
amber|Throwable|~Root of all thrown types|getMessage(), getCause()|the only thing you can throw/catch|parent of Error + Exception
rose|Error|~JVM-level failures|OutOfMemoryError|StackOverflowError|unchecked — do not catch
blue|Exception|~Recoverable conditions|IOException, SQLException|checked by default|must catch or declare with throws
emerald|RuntimeException|~The unchecked branch|NullPointerException|IllegalArgumentException|signals bugs — fix the code

sections.title: Walking the Hierarchy in Code
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Calling `Exception` the root.** `Throwable` is the root; `Exception` and `Error` are siblings beneath it.
- **Reading 'runtime' as timing.** Every exception is thrown at runtime. `RuntimeException` means *unchecked* — the compiler doesn't force handling.
- **Catching `Throwable` or `Error` 'to be safe'.** That swallows `OutOfMemoryError` and lets the app limp along in a broken JVM state.
- **Thinking checked vs unchecked is about severity.** It's purely a compiler rule about who must handle the exception, not how bad it is.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`Throwable` is the root** — the only type you can `throw` or `catch`; `Error` and `Exception` are its two children.
- **`Error` = JVM-level, unrecoverable** — `OutOfMemoryError`, `StackOverflowError`; don't catch them.
- **`Exception` = recoverable** — `IOException`, `SQLException`; checked unless it descends from `RuntimeException`.
- **`RuntimeException` = unchecked branch** — `NullPointerException`, `IllegalArgumentException`; usually signals a bug.
- **Checked vs unchecked is a compiler rule** layered on top of the hierarchy, not part of the class names' meaning.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: The thing I'd lead with is that the root of the hierarchy is Throwable, not Exception — that's the detail most people get wrong. Throwable is the only type you're actually allowed to throw or catch in Java, and it has two direct children. The first is Error, which represents serious JVM-level problems like running out of memory or blowing the stack with infinite recursion. Those aren't things your code can fix, so you don't catch them. The second is Exception, which represents conditions a normal program can anticipate and recover from, like a missing file throwing an I O exception or a bad query throwing a S Q L exception. Now, sitting underneath Exception there's a special subclass called RuntimeException, and that's the parent of all the unchecked exceptions, like NullPointerException or IllegalArgumentException. Everything else under Exception is checked, which means the compiler won't let you build until you either catch it or declare it with the throws keyword. One nuance I'd add is that the hierarchy and the checked-versus-unchecked rule are two separate ideas layered on top of each other. Both Error and RuntimeException are unchecked, but for opposite reasons — Error because recovery is hopeless, and RuntimeException because it usually means a bug you should just fix in the code rather than catch everywhere. And the word runtime is misleading, because every exception happens at runtime; here it just means unchecked.

questions.question: What is the difference between Error and Exception in Java?
questions.title: Error vs Exception in Java
questions.direct_answer: Both **`Error`** and **`Exception`** extend `Throwable`, but they signal different things. **`Error`** means the JVM itself is in trouble (`OutOfMemoryError`, `StackOverflowError`) — you normally let it crash the app. **`Exception`** means your program hit a recoverable condition (`IOException`, `SQLException`) you can catch and handle. The trap: never `catch (Throwable)` to 'handle everything', because that also swallows `Error`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand recoverability — that Error signals a broken JVM you let propagate, while Exception signals conditions your code can handle
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Catching Error (or Throwable) like a normal Exception, and assuming Errors only come from outside your code
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Point out StackOverflowError is caused by YOUR recursion yet you still shouldn't catch it — the fix is the code, not a catch block

sections.title: Two Branches of Throwable, Two Intentions
sections.content:
`Error` and `Exception` are the two direct subclasses of `Throwable`, and the difference is **recoverability**. An **`Error`** is the JVM's way of saying it's in serious trouble — the heap is exhausted (`OutOfMemoryError`) or the call stack is full (`StackOverflowError`). Catching it and continuing is dangerous because the JVM's state is undefined.

An **`Exception`** represents something your code can reasonably respond to: a file that doesn't exist, a network timeout, an invalid number. You can `catch` it, retry, or show a friendly message. The rule of thumb: **handle `Exception`s, let `Error`s propagate.**

sections.title: Error vs Exception
sections.content:
| Aspect | `Error` | `Exception` |
|---|---|---|
| Origin | JVM / environment | Application logic or external resources |
| Recoverable? | Almost never | Usually yes |
| Should you catch it? | No — let it crash | Yes, when you can act on it |
| Examples | `OutOfMemoryError`, `StackOverflowError` | `IOException`, `SQLException`, `NullPointerException` |
| Compiler treatment | Unchecked | Checked (unless it extends `RuntimeException`) |

sections.title: How to Treat Each Branch
sections.content:
rose|Error|~JVM is in trouble|OutOfMemoryError|StackOverflowError|let it propagate and crash
blue|Exception|~Program can react|IOException, SQLException|catch and recover|or wrap and rethrow
amber|The trap|~catch(Throwable) is wrong|swallows Error too|app runs broken|prefer catch(Exception)

sections.title: Wrong: catching Throwable hides JVM failures
Right: catch Exception, let Error escape
When to Handle Each
sections.content:
Catch an `Exception` subclass whenever your code can do something meaningful: retry an `IOException`, roll back a transaction on `SQLException`, or prompt the user after a `NumberFormatException`. Prefer the **most specific** type over a broad `catch (Exception)`.

For `Error`, the right move is almost always to do nothing and let it propagate to a top-level handler that logs and exits. The only place you see `catch (Throwable)` is framework code (servlet containers, thread pools) that must log a fatal failure before shutting the component down — and even then it terminates rather than continuing.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Both extend `Throwable`** but mean different things: `Error` = JVM broken, `Exception` = recoverable.
- **Let `Error` propagate** — catching `OutOfMemoryError` and continuing risks corrupt state.
- **`StackOverflowError` is your bug** (runaway recursion) yet still an `Error` — fix the recursion, don't catch it.
- **Never `catch (Throwable)`** in business code; it swallows `Error` along with `Exception`.
- **Prefer specific `Exception` types** over a blanket `catch (Exception)`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Both Error and Exception are direct subclasses of Throwable, so at the type level they look similar, but the intent behind them is completely different and it comes down to recoverability. An Error means the JVM itself is in trouble. The classic examples are OutOfMemoryError, where the heap is exhausted, and StackOverflowError, where the call stack is full. When you see one of those, there's usually nothing useful your application code can do, so the right response is to let it propagate and let the process crash, ideally so a supervisor can restart it cleanly. An Exception, on the other hand, represents a condition your program can reasonably anticipate and handle, like a missing file throwing an I O exception, or a failed database call throwing a S Q L exception. Those you can catch, maybe retry, maybe roll back a transaction, maybe show the user a friendly error. The biggest trap here is writing catch Throwable to, quote, handle everything. That's dangerous because Throwable is the parent of both, so you'd also be catching OutOfMemoryError and then continuing to run on a half-dead JVM, which can corrupt data. So in normal code I catch Exception, or even better a specific subclass, and I deliberately let Error escape. One subtle point worth mentioning is that StackOverflowError is actually caused by your own code, usually a recursion with no base case, but it's still classified as an Error, and the fix is to correct the recursion, not to wrap it in a catch block.

questions.question: Can you catch multiple exceptions in a single catch block in Java?
questions.title: Multi-Catch Exception Handling in Java 7
questions.direct_answer: Yes — since **Java 7**, **multi-catch** lets one `catch` handle several exception types using the pipe operator: `catch (IOException | SQLException e)`. It removes duplicated handling code. Two rules: the variable `e` is **implicitly `final`** (you can't reassign it), and the listed types **can't be parent-child** (`catch (Exception | IOException)` won't compile because it's redundant).

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of the Java 7 multi-catch syntax and its two compiler rules — implicitly final variable and the no-parent-child restriction
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing multi-catch exists and writing duplicate catch blocks, or trying to list a type and its supertype together
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain WHY the variable is final (the runtime type could be any of the listed types) and why parent-child is rejected as redundant

sections.title: One Catch Block for Many Exception Types
sections.content:
Before Java 7, if two exceptions needed identical handling you wrote two `catch` blocks with copy-pasted code. **Multi-catch**, added in Java 7, lets you list several types in one block separated by the **pipe operator** `|`: `catch (IOException | SQLException e)`. The same body runs for either type.

Two compiler rules matter. First, the variable `e` is **implicitly `final`** — you can't reassign it inside the block. Second, the listed types **must not be in a parent-child relationship**: `catch (Exception | IOException e)` is a compile error because `Exception` already covers `IOException`, making the second type redundant. The static type of `e` is the nearest common supertype of everything you listed.

sections.title: Multi-Catch at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|Syntax|~Pipe between types|catch (A \| B e)|since Java 7|same body for all listed types
amber|Variable is final|~Can't reassign e|runtime type is any of them|so e is read-only|compiler enforces it
rose|No parent-child|~Redundant = error|catch (Exception \| IOException)|won't compile|list independent types only
blue|Static type|~Nearest common parent|IOException \| SQLException -> Exception|use only shared methods|getMessage() is safe

sections.title: Without multi-catch: duplicated handling
With multi-catch: one block, one source of truth
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not knowing it exists** — writing N identical catch blocks instead of one multi-catch.
- **Listing a type and its supertype** — `catch (Exception | IOException)` is a compile error (redundant).
- **Trying to reassign `e`** — it's implicitly `final`; `e = new ...` won't compile.
- **Forcing unrelated exceptions together** — if `IOException` should retry but `SQLException` should fail, keep separate blocks; multi-catch is only for *identical* handling.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Multi-catch (Java 7+)** uses `|` to handle several types in one block.
- **The variable is implicitly `final`** — no reassignment inside the block.
- **No parent-child types** — listing a supertype with its subtype is a compile error.
- **Static type of `e`** is the nearest common ancestor of the listed types.
- **Use it only for identical handling** — different responses still need separate blocks.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Yes, and the feature is called multi-catch — it arrived in Java 7. The idea is that instead of writing two separate catch blocks with the same body, you list the exception types in a single catch separated by a pipe character, like catch I O exception pipe number format exception. Then that one block handles either type, which removes the copy-paste duplication you'd otherwise have. There are two rules the interviewer is usually probing for. The first is that the caught variable is implicitly final, so you can't reassign it inside the block. The reason is that at runtime the actual exception could be any of the listed types, so Java treats the variable as read-only to keep things unambiguous. The second rule is that the types you list can't be in a parent-child relationship. If you write catch exception pipe I O exception, that's a compile error, because I O exception is already a subclass of exception, so listing both is redundant. You can only combine types that are independent branches of the hierarchy. One more detail worth knowing is that the static type of the variable is the nearest common supertype of everything you listed, so if you combine two unrelated checked exceptions you'll effectively be working with Exception, and you can only call methods that exist on that common parent, like getMessage. The practical guidance I'd give is to use multi-catch only when the handling is genuinely identical. If one exception should trigger a retry and another should fail immediately, keep them in separate catch blocks so the intent stays clear.

questions.question: What is RuntimeException and why is it special in the hierarchy?
questions.title: RuntimeException in Java Hierarchy
questions.direct_answer: **`RuntimeException`** is a subclass of `Exception` and the parent of all **unchecked** exceptions. Because it's unchecked, the compiler never forces you to declare it with `throws` or catch it. Its subclasses — `NullPointerException`, `IllegalArgumentException`, `IllegalStateException` — typically signal **programming bugs** you should fix, not external failures you should handle. 'Runtime' means *unchecked*, not 'happens at runtime'.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the checked vs unchecked split and why unchecked exceptions exist — to avoid forcing try-catch around every line for bugs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reading 'RuntimeException' as 'exceptions that occur at runtime', and broadly catching RuntimeException instead of fixing the underlying bug
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that unchecked = the compiler trusts you to fix bugs, while checked = the compiler insists you plan for external failures

sections.title: Why RuntimeException Gets a Compiler Free Pass
sections.content:
**`RuntimeException`** is a direct subclass of `Exception`, but the compiler treats it and everything beneath it specially: they're **unchecked**. You can throw a `NullPointerException` or `IllegalArgumentException` without declaring `throws`, and callers don't have to catch them.

Why the exemption? Because `RuntimeException` subclasses usually mean a **bug in the code**: a `NullPointerException` means you forgot a null check, an `IndexOutOfBoundsException` means your loop bounds are wrong. If the compiler forced try-catch around every array access and method call, code would be unreadable. The right response to these is to *fix the logic*, not catch and continue. Checked exceptions, by contrast, model genuine external failures (a file is gone, the network dropped) where recovering makes sense — so the compiler insists you handle them. And note: 'runtime' here means *unchecked*; all exceptions are thrown at runtime.

sections.title: Checked vs Unchecked, and Where RuntimeException Sits
sections.content:
emerald|RuntimeException|~The unchecked branch|no throws needed|callers needn't catch|usually means a bug
amber|Common subclasses|~Bugs to fix in code|NullPointerException|IllegalArgumentException|IndexOutOfBoundsException
blue|Checked exceptions|~External failures|IOException, SQLException|compiler forces handling|recovery is meaningful
rose|Name trap|~'Runtime' = unchecked|every exception is at runtime|not about timing|it's a compiler rule

sections.title: Unchecked Means No throws Required
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking 'runtime' = timing.** All exceptions occur at runtime; the word means *unchecked*.
- **Broadly catching `RuntimeException`.** That hides `NullPointerException`s and other bugs instead of fixing them — let them fail fast.
- **Making genuine bugs into checked exceptions.** Forcing callers to handle a programming error clutters code; use unchecked for misuse.
- **Forgetting `RuntimeException` is still an `Exception`.** `catch (Exception e)` also catches unchecked ones.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`RuntimeException` = parent of all unchecked exceptions**, and itself a subclass of `Exception`.
- **Unchecked = no `throws`, no forced catch** — the compiler stays out of your way.
- **It usually signals a bug** — `NullPointerException`, `IllegalArgumentException`, `IllegalStateException`.
- **'Runtime' means unchecked**, not 'occurs at runtime' — every exception does.
- **Don't catch it broadly** — fix the root cause and let bugs fail fast.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: RuntimeException is a direct subclass of Exception, but what makes it special is how the compiler treats it: it and all of its subclasses are unchecked. That means you can throw something like IllegalArgumentException without adding a throws clause to your method, and any code that calls you isn't forced to wrap it in a try-catch. The reason this exemption exists comes down to the kind of problem these exceptions represent. RuntimeException subclasses almost always indicate a bug in the code rather than an external failure. A NullPointerException means somebody forgot a null check, an index out of bounds means the loop bounds are wrong. If the compiler forced you to catch those everywhere, you'd have try-catch blocks around every line and the code would be unreadable. The intended response to a bug is to fix the logic, not to catch it and keep going. Compare that to checked exceptions like I O exception or S Q L exception, which model genuine external failures — a file is missing, the network dropped — where catching and recovering actually makes sense, so the compiler insists you handle them. The biggest naming trap is that people read the word runtime as meaning these happen at runtime as opposed to some other time, but every exception in Java is thrown at runtime. Here, runtime just means unchecked. So when I design my own exceptions, I extend RuntimeException for things that represent misuse or precondition violations, like a null argument, and I reserve checked exceptions for recoverable external conditions. And I avoid catching RuntimeException broadly, because that just hides bugs I'd rather see fail fast.

How do you decide whether to make a custom exception checked or unchecked?

questions.question: What methods does the Throwable class provide?
questions.title: Throwable Class Methods in Java
questions.direct_answer: `Throwable` provides the shared machinery every exception inherits: **`getMessage()`** returns the description, **`getCause()`** returns the wrapped underlying exception (enabling **exception chaining**), **`printStackTrace()`** dumps the call stack to `stderr`, **`getStackTrace()`** returns the frames as an array for logging frameworks, and **`addSuppressed()`/`getSuppressed()`** carry extra exceptions (used by try-with-resources).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know Throwable is more than a marker — it carries the diagnostic methods, especially getCause for exception chaining
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing getCause exists, so wrapping an exception without passing the original and losing the root cause in production
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Stress that preserving the cause chain is what makes a production stack trace debuggable, and contrast printStackTrace with logging via getStackTrace

sections.title: Throwable Is the Diagnostic Engine of Exceptions
sections.content:
`Throwable` isn't just the root type — it implements the methods every exception relies on. **`getMessage()`** returns the human-readable text you passed to the constructor. **`getCause()`** returns the underlying exception that triggered this one, which is the foundation of **exception chaining**: you wrap a low-level error (say `SQLException`) inside a domain error (`OrderLookupException`) while keeping the original as the cause.

**`printStackTrace()`** writes the full call stack to `System.err` — handy in development, but in production you log via a framework instead. **`getStackTrace()`** returns the same information as a `StackTraceElement[]` so loggers can format it. **`addSuppressed()`/`getSuppressed()`** carry secondary exceptions, which is how try-with-resources records a failure from `close()` without losing the primary one.

sections.title: Key Throwable Methods
sections.content:
amber|getMessage()|~The description|text you passed to constructor|null if none given|first thing you log
blue|getCause()|~Exception chaining|the wrapped original|preserves root cause|null if not chained
emerald|getStackTrace()|~Frames as array|StackTraceElement[]|used by loggers|programmatic access
rose|printStackTrace()|~Dumps to stderr|good for quick dev checks|bypasses log framework|avoid in production

sections.title: Wrong: wrapping without the cause loses the root error
Right: chain the cause so the trace stays debuggable
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Wrapping without the cause** — `throw new XException(msg)` instead of `throw new XException(msg, e)` discards the root cause.
- **Using `printStackTrace()` in production** — it writes to `stderr`, bypassing your log framework; log the exception object instead.
- **Never walking `getCause()`** — the real diagnostic info is often several layers down the chain.
- **Confusing `getMessage()` with `toString()`** — `toString()` includes the class name; `getMessage()` is just the text.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`getMessage()`** — the description string; **`getCause()`** — the wrapped original (exception chaining).
- **Always pass the cause** when wrapping: `new XException(msg, original)`.
- **`getStackTrace()`** for structured logging; **`printStackTrace()`** only for quick local debugging.
- **`addSuppressed()`/`getSuppressed()`** record secondary failures — used automatically by try-with-resources.
- **Preserving the cause chain** is what makes production failures debuggable without a debugger.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Throwable is the root of the exception hierarchy, but it's also where all the diagnostic plumbing lives, so every exception inherits these methods. The most basic one is getMessage, which returns the human-readable description you passed into the constructor. The one I'd really emphasise, because freshers often miss it, is getCause. That returns the underlying exception that triggered this one, and it's the basis of exception chaining. Say your data layer throws a S Q L exception but your service layer wants to throw its own domain exception — you pass the S Q L exception in as the cause, so later anyone can call getCause and recover the original error, including the database error code. If you don't preserve that cause, you've thrown away the information you'll need to debug the problem in production. Then there's printStackTrace, which everyone knows from tutorials — it dumps the full call stack to standard error. That's fine for a quick local check, but in production you shouldn't use it because it bypasses your logging framework. Instead you use getStackTrace, which gives you the stack frames as an array of StackTraceElement objects that a logger can format properly. There's also addSuppressed and getSuppressed, which carry secondary exceptions; that's how try-with-resources records a failure from closing a resource without losing the primary exception. The big mistake to avoid is wrapping an exception and forgetting to pass the original as the cause, because then the chain is broken and your logs show the wrapper but not the actual reason. When I debug, I walk the cause chain by calling getCause repeatedly, because the real culprit is often a few layers down.

questions.question: Does the finally block run even when an exception is not caught?
questions.title: Finally Block Execution Without Catch
questions.direct_answer: Yes. **`finally` always runs**, even when the exception isn't caught — it executes *before* the exception continues propagating up the stack, and even before a `return` actually returns. The only times it doesn't run are **`System.exit()`** or a JVM crash. Watch out: if `finally` itself throws (or `return`s), it **replaces/suppresses the original exception**, losing the real error.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know finally runs regardless of whether the exception is caught, and the precise edge cases where it doesn't or where it hides the original exception
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking finally only runs when there's a matching catch, or that it runs after the exception has already left the method
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name System.exit() as the escape hatch and explain how a throw or return inside finally silently swallows the original exception

sections.title: finally: The Block That Almost Always Runs
sections.content:
The **`finally`** block is Java's guarantee for cleanup — close a file, release a lock, reset state — and it runs whether or not an exception occurred, and whether or not that exception was caught. If an exception is thrown and there's no matching `catch`, the `finally` block still executes **first**, and only then does the exception continue propagating up the call stack.

It even runs when the `try` or `catch` has a `return`: the return value is computed, `finally` runs, then the method actually returns. There are exactly two ways to skip it: calling **`System.exit()`**, or the JVM dying (a hard crash). The dangerous part is that if `finally` throws an exception or has its own `return`, it **overrides** whatever the `try` block was doing — silently swallowing the original exception.

sections.title: Does finally Run? Decision Flow
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[try block runs] --> B{Exception
thrown?} B -- No --> C[try finishes] B -- Yes --> D{Matching
catch?} D -- Yes --> E[catch runs] D -- No --> F[exception pending] C --> G[[finally runs]] E --> G F --> G G --> H{System.exit
or JVM crash?} H -- No, normal --> I[return value / propagate exception] H -- Yes --> J[finally skipped / process dies] ```

sections.title: finally Runs Before the Exception Escapes
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming `finally` needs a `catch`.** It runs even with zero catch blocks — the exception just propagates afterward.
- **Throwing from `finally`.** A new exception there replaces the original `try` exception, destroying the real diagnostic info.
- **`return` inside `finally`.** It silently overrides the `try`/`catch` return value — a classic interview gotcha.
- **Expecting it after `System.exit()`.** That's the one normal case where `finally` is skipped.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`finally` runs whether or not the exception is caught** — and before the exception propagates.
- **It runs before a `return`** completes, on both success and failure paths.
- **Skipped only by `System.exit()` or a JVM crash.**
- **A `throw` or `return` in `finally` overrides/suppresses** the original exception or return value.
- **Prefer try-with-resources** for cleanup — it avoids the swallowed-exception trap automatically.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Yes, the finally block runs even when the exception isn't caught — that's really the whole point of it. It's Java's guarantee that cleanup code executes no matter what happens in the try block. The execution order is the part people get wrong, so let me be precise. If an exception is thrown and there's no matching catch, the finally block still runs first, and only after it finishes does the exception continue propagating up the call stack. So finally runs before the exception leaves the method. It also runs even when you have a return statement — the return value gets computed, then finally executes, then the method actually returns. There are exactly two situations where finally does not run. The first is if you call System dot exit, which stops the JVM immediately. The second is if the JVM itself crashes hard, like a fatal native error. Outside of those, finally always runs. Now the dangerous part, and this is what interviewers like to probe: if the finally block itself throws an exception, that new exception replaces the original one from the try block, and you lose the real error. The same thing happens if you put a return statement inside finally — it silently overrides whatever the try or catch was going to return. So the rule I follow is to keep finally blocks simple and never throw or return from them. And for resource cleanup specifically, I prefer try-with-resources, because it handles closing automatically and, instead of losing the original exception, it attaches the close failure as a suppressed exception so you keep both.

beats.text: The finally block is Java's guarantee of cleanup. It runs after the try (and catch, if present) regardless of what happened — exception thrown, exception caught, or normal exit. It's designed for code that must execute no matter the outcome.

Without finally, cleanup code like closing connections or releasing locks would only run on the happy path. If an exception skipped past it, you'd have resource leaks. Finally was designed to close that gap.

items: Runs after try completes — whether normally or by exception
Runs even when no catch block matches the exception
Does NOT run if System.exit() is called or the JVM crashes
If finally itself throws, the original exception is silently replaced

beats.text: sharp edge: If your finally block throws a new exception, Java discards the original exception completely. In a Java 17 service, if close() on a resource throws inside finally, you lose the original failure reason — one reason try-with-resources is preferred over manual finally blocks.

items: Putting a return statement in finally — it overrides the try block's return value silently.
Assuming finally doesn't run without a catch — it runs even with zero catch blocks.
Letting finally throw — it silently swallows the original exception you actually need to diagnose.
